clinicalPearls: A group of autosomal recessive disorders of adrenal steroid synthesis, the great majority caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
The classic salt-wasting form presents in the first weeks of life with vomiting, poor feeding, weight loss, dehydration, and shock from combined cortisol and aldosterone deficiency.

Female infants with the classic form often show virilisation of the external genitalia (ambiguous genitalia), whereas affected males may appear normal at birth and are at particular risk of unrecognised salt-wasting crisis.
Characteristic biochemistry includes hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and metabolic acidosis in the salt-wasting crisis, with markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
A non-classic (late-onset) form presents later with signs of androgen excess such as premature pubarche, hirsutism, or menstrual irregularity.
Newborn screening measuring 17-hydroxyprogesterone allows early detection before a life-threatening crisis.

Treatment principle is glucocorticoid replacement to correct cortisol deficiency and suppress excess adrenal androgen, with mineralocorticoid replacement (and salt supplementation in infancy) for salt-wasting forms.
Additional stress steroid cover is essential during illness, surgery, or major stress to prevent adrenal crisis.
Management of affected girls includes multidisciplinary care regarding virilised genitalia, and genetic counselling is important for families.
reference.pathophysiology: A deficiency of an enzyme in the adrenal cortisol synthesis pathway, most often 21-hydroxylase, reduces cortisol production. The resulting loss of negative feedback drives increased ACTH secretion, which stimulates adrenal hyperplasia and diverts steroid precursors into the androgen pathway, causing androgen excess and virilisation. In the severe salt-wasting form, aldosterone synthesis is also impaired, leading to sodium loss, hyperkalaemia, and volume depletion, while accumulation of the precursor 17-hydroxyprogesterone serves as a diagnostic marker.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of ambiguous genitalia and disorders of sex development
Pyloric stenosis or sepsis in a vomiting, dehydrated neonate
Other forms of primary adrenal insufficiency
additionalInvestigations: Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (baseline and, if needed, after ACTH stimulation)
Serum electrolytes, glucose, and acid-base status
Karyotype and pelvic ultrasound in ambiguous genitalia
Genetic analysis of the CYP21A2 gene
redFlags: Salt-wasting adrenal crisis with dehydration, hypotension, or shock
Vomiting and poor feeding in a neonate, particularly a male infant
Intercurrent illness or surgery without adequate stress steroid cover
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, hormone replacement, and stress dosing, children generally grow and develop well; risks include life-threatening adrenal crises, effects of over- or under-treatment on growth and puberty, and fertility and psychosocial issues in classic disease.
pitfalls: Missing salt-wasting crisis in a male infant with normal genitalia
Failing to provide stress steroid cover during illness or surgery
Over-treating with glucocorticoids, impairing growth, or under-treating, allowing androgen excess
Misattributing a neonatal collapse to sepsis or pyloric stenosis without checking electrolytes and adrenal steroids
